paragraphs.heading: Splitting a nucleus
paragraphs.text: In nuclear fission, an atom's nucleus breaks apart into two or more smaller nuclei. The pieces, called fragments or daughter atoms, are different elements from the parent, which makes fission a kind of nuclear transmutation. For common fissile isotopes the two pieces are usually close in size but not equal, often with masses in a ratio of about 3 to 2. Now and then, 2 to 4 times in every 1000 events, three charged pieces come out instead, which is called ternary fission.

paragraphs.heading: Where the energy comes from
paragraphs.text: Fission often gives off neutrons and gamma rays, and it releases a huge amount of energy, large even next to other radioactive decay. Splitting one uranium-235 atom frees roughly 100 million times the energy of burning one carbon atom in air to make CO₂. For heavy nuclides this energy comes out as electromagnetic radiation and as motion of the fragments, which heats the material. Two things are needed: the products must have more total binding energy than the starting nucleus, and the fission barrier must be overcome.

paragraphs.heading: A wobbling drop
paragraphs.text: Bohr and Wheeler used a liquid drop model to estimate the mass difference between parent and daughter nuclei, then turned the mass difference into energy with Einstein's mass-energy formula. They likened a nucleus struck by a neutron to a vibrating drop, with surface tension and the Coulomb force working against each other. When they plotted the energy as the drop stretched, the result had a saddle shape. That saddle forms a hurdle called the critical energy barrier, and about 6 MeV from the incoming neutron was needed to get over it.

paragraphs.heading: Chain reactions
paragraphs.text: A splitting nucleus releases more neutrons than the one it took in, so a chain reaction is possible. Fissile nuclides split easily when hit by slow, or thermal, neutrons. Three isotopes, U-233, U-235 and Pu-239, can sustain a chain reaction. Nuclear power plants run in a delayed critical state so the energy comes out under control, while nuclear weapons use a prompt supercritical state that releases it uncontrolled in about a microsecond. Nuclides that can keep a chain reaction going are suitable as nuclear fuels.

paragraphs.heading: Discovery in 1938
paragraphs.text: Fission was discovered by the chemists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann and the physicists Lise Meitner and Otto Robert Frisch. Hahn and Strassmann proved on 19 December 1938 that the reaction had happened, and Meitner and her nephew Frisch explained it in theory in January 1939. Frisch borrowed the word fission from biology, where living cells divide. In February 1939 Hahn and Strassmann predicted that the process frees extra neutrons, which opened the way to a chain reaction in a critical mass of fissile material.

paragraphs.heading: Fission without a push
paragraphs.text: Fission does not always need a neutron to start it. Spontaneous fission, which Georgy Flyorov, Konstantin Petrzhak and Igor Kurchatov discovered in 1940, is a form of radioactive decay in isotopes of very high mass number, whose nuclei are already unstable from too many neutrons. Unlike fusion, which powers stars, fission can be considered negligible in how the universe evolved. Even so, natural fission reactors have formed under very rare conditions.
